f_bio.text:
(1-5)

Bioluminescence is the production and emission of light by living organisms. It occurs widely in the ocean, where an estimated 76 percent of animals living in the water column can produce light. The chemical reaction behind the glow usually involves a light-emitting molecule called luciferin and an enzyme, luciferase, that speeds up its oxidation. Organisms use bioluminescence for a variety of purposes. Anglerfish dangle a glowing lure to attract prey, while certain squid release a luminous cloud to confuse predators, much as other squid squirt ink. In some species, such as the firefly, flashing patterns help individuals identify potential mates. Although land-based bioluminescent organisms exist, they are far less common; fireflies and certain fungi are the best-known examples.

f_heat.text:
(6-9)

Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and tar roofs absorb more sunlight than natural vegetation does, and they release that stored heat slowly after sunset. In addition, tall buildings block wind that might otherwise carry heat away, and air conditioners and vehicles add waste heat to the air. The consequences extend beyond discomfort: higher temperatures increase electricity demand and can worsen air pollution. Planners have responded with several strategies, including painting roofs white, planting trees along streets, and creating rooftop gardens. Studies suggest that these measures can reduce local temperatures by one to three degrees Celsius, although the results vary by climate and neighborhood.

f_econ.text:
(10-13)

Economists use the concept of comparative advantage to explain why trade benefits both parties even when one is better at producing everything. Suppose that Country A can produce either 10 cars or 20 tons of wheat in a year using all its resources, while Country B can produce either 4 cars or 16 tons of wheat. Country A is more efficient at both, an advantage economists call absolute advantage. However, Country A gives up 2 tons of wheat for each car, whereas Country B gives up 4 tons of wheat per car. Country A therefore has a comparative advantage in cars, since its opportunity cost is lower, and Country B in wheat. If each country specializes in what it does relatively better and then trades, total output can rise.

f_sleep.text:
(14-17)

Researchers have long suspected that sleep plays a role in memory, and experiments over the past two decades have provided substantial support for this idea. In one study, participants learned a list of word pairs in the evening. Half were allowed to sleep normally, while the other half stayed awake all night. After two nights of recovery sleep for everyone, both groups were tested; those who had slept the first night recalled significantly more word pairs. Scientists believe that during deep sleep the brain replays recent experiences, strengthening the neural connections that represent them. Even a short nap of an hour or so has been shown to help.

f_coral.text:
(18-21)

Coral reefs depend on a partnership. Tiny algae called zooxanthellae live inside coral tissue, providing up to 90 percent of the coral's energy through photosynthesis in exchange for shelter. When the water becomes too warm, the coral expels the algae, and without the algae its tissue becomes transparent, revealing the white skeleton beneath. This is known as bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. If temperatures return to normal quickly, algae can recolonize the coral and it can recover; prolonged heat, however, causes the coral to die. Mass bleaching events were rare before the 1980s but have become more frequent as ocean temperatures have risen.

f_print.text:
(22-25)

Before the mid-fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, a slow and costly process that made them rare luxuries. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg introduced a printing system using movable metal type, which allowed a printer to assemble pages from reusable letters. Although the Chinese had earlier developed movable type, Gutenberg's design, combined with an oil-based ink and a modified wine press, proved especially well suited to the Latin alphabet, which has relatively few characters. Within fifty years, printing presses operated in more than 250 European cities, and the price of books fell dramatically. Historians argue that this wider availability of printed material accelerated literacy and the spread of new ideas, including those of the Protestant Reformation.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Bioluminescence is a chemical process that living things use for several purposes, mostly in the ocean
Anglerfish are the most important bioluminescent animals
Luciferin is found only in deep-sea animals
Fireflies are the only land animals that produce light

questions.q: According to the passage, what is the function of luciferase?
options: It attracts prey toward the organism
It stores energy for later use
It protects the organism from predators
It speeds up the reaction that produces light

questions.q: The word "luminous" in the passage is closest in meaning to

enormous
sticky
glowing

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a use of bioluminescence?

Attracting prey
Confusing predators

questions.q: What can be inferred from the passage about bioluminescence?
options: It is more common in the ocean than on land
It is found only in animals
It evolved first in fungi
It requires sunlight to work
